Much, Many & the Day Spain Went Dark

⚡
📖 The story

Read me first!

On Monday, April 28, 2025, at 12:33 p.m., the lights went out in Spain and Portugal. In five seconds, the grid lost 15 gigawatts: 60% of the electricity the country was using at that moment. Almost 60 million people had no power. How much electricity was that? More than the production of fifteen nuclear reactors.

Trains and subways stopped. Rescue teams helped about 35,000 passengers who were stuck in trains. Traffic lights didn't work, phones didn't work, and many shops couldn't accept cards, so people needed cash. Hospitals didn't lose power: they ran on backup generators.

It wasn't a cyberattack. That morning, the voltage was unstable, and it rose too high in the south of Spain. Several power plants disconnected to protect their equipment. Each disconnection pushed the voltage higher, so many more plants tripped: a chain reaction. Finally, the Iberian grid separated from Europe and collapsed. Why? There weren't enough plants controlling the voltage, and too much of the electricity came from solar farms that didn't control it.

Engineers didn't have much time. They began a "black start": they restarted the hydroelectric plants first, France and Morocco sent power through the interconnections, and they reconnected the regions one by one. By the next morning, almost all of Spain had power again.

Much or many? — the rule

MANYMUCHA LOT OF
avec…un nom au pluriel (on peut compter)
plants · people · passengers · hours		 un nom indénombrable (pas de pluriel)
electricity · time · money · information · power		 les deux
questionHow many passengers were stuck?How much electricity was that?—
négationThere weren't many plants.Engineers didn't have much time.—
positifMany shops closed. (écrit)Too much electricity came from solar.A lot of plants tripped. (oral, le plus courant)

👉 Réflexe : many = je peux compter (3 plants, 4 hours) · much = je ne peux pas (electricity, time) · à l'oral et au positif, a lot of marche presque toujours.

B2 words — the right term

6 pts

👉 Un mot du vocabulaire B2 par phrase.

  1. Big rotating machines give the grid standby a surge inertia , which slows down frequency changes.
  2. Before reconnecting a region, engineers must trip curtail synchronize its frequency with the rest of the grid.
  3. Cutting power to some areas on purpose to save the grid is called redundancy inertia load shedding .
  4. When the voltage is too high, the protection relay curtails trips synchronizes the breaker.
  5. A sudden, short rise in voltage is an outage a surge a substation .
  6. A second line that does the same job as the main line is a surge load shedding redundancy .
